pharm: Synthetic topical glucocorticoid with anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions; acts via induction of lipocortins that inhibit phospholipase A2
quick: Apply thin layer once or twice daily; max 2 weeks, <=50 g/week
Category C; use only if benefit justifies fetal risk
Caution; systemic corticosteroids appear in milk
HPA axis (ACTH stimulation, AM cortisol) with large area/prolonged use
summary: Halobetasol propionate 0.05% is a super-high-potency (Class I) topical corticosteroid for relief of inflammatory and pruritic corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. Treatment is limited to two consecutive weeks and a total of no more than 50 g per week because of the risk of HPA-axis suppression. It should not be used under occlusion and is not recommended in children under 12 years.
indications: Relief of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer to affected skin once or twice daily; rub in gently
dosage.n: Do not use with occlusive dressings; discontinue when control achieved
Higher skin-surface-to-body-mass ratio increases HPA suppression risk

admin: Apply a thin layer and rub in gently and completely
Do not use with occlusive dressings
Do not exceed 2 consecutive weeks or 50 g per week
Treat only small areas; discontinue when control is achieved
Reassess diagnosis if no improvement within 2 weeks
Avoid application to face, groin, or axillae unless directed; wash hands after use
moa: Like other topical corticosteroids, halobetasol propionate has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions. It is thought to act by inducing phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins (lipocortins), which control biosynthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting release of their precursor arachidonic acid.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to halobetasol propionate or any component of the preparation
relative: Application to large surface areas or under occlusion
Use beyond 2 weeks or more than 50 g/week
monitor: Signs of HPA-axis suppression with extensive or prolonged use

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Corticosteroids are teratogenic in laboratory animals when given systemically at low doses, and halobetasol propionate was teratogenic in rats and rabbits (cleft palate; omphalocele in rats) at multiples of the human topical dose. There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk and could suppress growth, interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production, or cause other untoward effects. It is not known whether topical application produces sufficient systemic absorption to be detectable in milk. Exercise caution when used in a nursing woman.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is described; systemic absorption is low (less than 6% of an applied dose over 96 hours). Extensive or occluded application increases absorption and systemic risk.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described given minimal systemic absorption with appropriate use.

interactions.diagnostics: Systemic absorption can affect HPA-axis testing; ACTH stimulation, AM plasma cortisol, and urinary free-cortisol tests are used to assess HPA suppression

common: Stinging or burning at the application site
serious: HPA-axis suppression with glucocorticoid insufficiency on withdrawal
Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, glucosuria from systemic absorption
rare: Perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, secondary infection, miliaria
In children: linear growth retardation, delayed weight gain, intracranial hypertension
emergency: Adrenal crisis from HPA-axis suppression after withdrawal
Intracranial hypertension in children (bulging fontanelles, headache, papilledema)

monitoring: Periodic evaluation for HPA-axis suppression with large-area or occlusive use (ACTH stimulation, AM cortisol, urinary free-cortisol)
Local skin reactions (atrophy, striae, irritation, secondary infection)
Growth in pediatric patients if used
Treatment duration and total weekly amount
counsel: Use only as directed; do not exceed 2 weeks or 50 g per week
Apply a thin layer to affected areas only; do not bandage or cover unless told to
Report skin irritation, thinning, or failure to improve
Do not use in children under 12 years
Avoid the face, underarms, and groin unless your doctor directs
Wash hands after applying unless treating the hands
pk: Anti-inflammatory effect develops over days of topical use
Not characterized for clinical effect; super-high potency class
HPA effects reversible; recovery generally prompt after discontinuation
pearls: Super-high (Class I) potency - limit to 2 weeks and <=50 g/week
Never use under occlusive dressings (increases absorption)
Produced HPA-axis suppression at 7 g/day for one week in psoriasis patients
Not recommended under age 12; children at higher risk of systemic effects
Allergic contact dermatitis presents as failure to heal rather than worsening - confirm with patch testing
missed: If you miss an application, apply it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next application, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Topically applied halobetasol can be absorbed in amounts sufficient to produce systemic effects (HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, features of Cushing's syndrome). Discontinue or reduce frequency, or substitute a less potent corticosteroid; supplemental systemic corticosteroids may rarely be needed if glucocorticoid insufficiency occurs.
